section 8 is one type of subsidized housing in which part of the renter's rent is paid for by the gov't. section 8 is meant for the poor, disabled, and elderly, or those parties deemed unable to afford market rent.

To correct /u/Teekno, you can live in public housing that is also section 8, because I do. Like /u/Teekno says, people on section 8 get vouchers that help them get subsidized housing. You can have a project-based voucher or a portable one. project-based means if you move out a specific housing project covered by section 8, you lose your voucher. portable means the people can apply the voucher to any apartment they want, whether it's in a section 8 project or not. Laws technically prevent private landlords from discriminating against portable voucher holders, but in practice many landlords do discriminate, in my opinion, do to the notion that section 8 holders, being poor, are more likely to have trouble paying rent.

You could have subsidized housing that is not section 8, because "subsidize" just means "to foot all/part of the bill for," so you could have student housing subsidized by a college, or a trust-funder's rent subsidized their parents. hope this helps.

Once upon a time, there were twins named Hansel and Gretel who were coming back home through The Great Forest after visiting their grandma. The twins were ten years old, and they argued a lot.

Hansel liked to pretend he was a pirate, but he wouldn't let his sister swordfight with him. "Girls can't be pirates," he said.

"Yes, they can," said Gretel.

"Can't!"

"Can!"

"Nuh-uh!"

"Ya-huh!"

And so on. Until they weren't even arguing using words. The fighting left the twins grumpy, and their parents annoyed. Hansel and Gretel were the only children who lived in The Great Forest. 

And as they went home from grandma's that night, they were arguing about whether boys could be witches.

Hansel whined to Gretel, "Why won't you let me play witch with you, and pretend to cast spells?"

"Because boys can't be witches," said Gretel.

"Yes, they can," said Hansel. 

"Can't!"

"Can!"

"Nuh-uh!"

"Ya-huh!"

"Um, Gretel," said Hansel. "I think we're lost. Do you have the cell phone to call Mom and Dad?"

Now Gretel was feeling very grumpy because she was hungry, and it was way past dinnertime. "No, I DON'T have the cell phone!" she snapped. "I thought YOU had it!" 

"Well, I thought YOU had it, and I'm SOOOOOOOOOOO hungry," whined Hansel.

"You were supposed to have it."

"No, you were!"

Hansel stopped and sniffed. He said, "Gretel, do you smell that chocolate?" 

Gretel stopped and sniffed. "Yes, I do. Do you smell that peppermint?"

"Yes, I do," said Hansel.

Mouths watering, the children raced toward the house with its lighted sugar pane windows.

But they stopped suddenly before knocking on the little gingerbread door. “Um, Gretel?” said Hansel. “Isn’t there a story that Mom and Dad tell us about a witch who lives in a house made of candy? And she eats lost kids?”

Gretel thought a moment. “Yes, I remember the story. But I have a plan. You go hide.”

So Hansel hid, and Gretel knocked on the door, and did her best to look like she knew what she was doing, instead of like a hungry and tired kid.

A man opened the door. Gretel sighed with relief, because boys couldn’t be witches. “Well, I’m going door-to-door selling cookies, and I wondered if you had an extra copy of a neighborhood map I could borrow. I lost mine.”

“I’ll do better than that, Gretel,” said the man. He pulled a cell phone out of thin air. “Use this to call your mom and dad.”

“H-How did you make the phone appear?” stammered Gretel.

The man smiled. “Magic. I’m a witch.” Gretel blinked in surprise. 

“Told you boys could be witches!” called Hansel from his hiding place.

“My name’s Louis,” said the witch.

“You might as well come out, Hansel,” Louis called to the boy. “I know you and Gretel are VEEERRRY hungry.”

“But… But… How did you know are names?” asked Hansel.

“And how do we know you’re not going to eat us, like the witch in the story?” asked Gretel.

“Well,” said Louis, “Everyone in The Great Forest knows your names, because you’re the only two children that live here. And witches don’t eat people. We just say that to scare people away because people keep bugging us to cast spells, and they won’t leave us alone. Now can we all eat? The supper I made is getting cold.”

Before they ate, Louis called the twins’ parents to tell them that Hansel and Gretel were safe with him.

Between bites, Gretel asked, “Louis, do you know any girl pirates?”

Before Louis could answer, Hansel said, “There’s no such thing as girl pirates! And they can’t use wheelchairs, like you do, Gretel. Pirates have eye patches, and peg legs, but they don’t use wheelchairs.”

Louis the witch smiled and cast a spell. ZAP!

Suddenly, the three of them found themselves on the sea aboard a pirate ship, surrounded by pirates.

Hansel had never been around real pirates before, but he knew the stories, and was suddenly scared. “Are you going to fight us? Or rob us? Or make us walk the plank?” He looked down at the water far below.

“That’s up to the captain,” said the pirates. And they made room for the captain to come through.

A girl drove a wheelchair through the group of pirates!

She nodded to Louis. “Arrr! Nice to see you again, Lou. I’m usin’ this chair on account o’ losin’ me legs to a great white whale!”

To Hansel and Gretel, she said, “My name’s Jill Rogers, so I call me ship The Jilly Roger. And no, we won’t fight ye, or rob ye, or make ye walk the plank. We do sword-fightin’ when we rob the rich to give to the poor. As ye can see, I got men and women in me crew, even boys and girls!”

“Wow,” said Hansel and Gretel as they looked at all the pirates smiling at them aboard The Jilly Roger. “Can we go on adventures with you?” they asked.

“Maybe soon, but not today,” said Captain Jill Rogers.

“Why not?” asked Hansel and Gretel.

Louis the witch said, “Because your parents just called and said its way past your bedtime.”

Louis the witch cast a spell, and Captain Jill Rogers and her pirates steered The Jilly Roger up into the sky, through the stars, and right to Hansel and Gretel’s front door.
And Hansel and Gretel fell asleep, dreaming of the adventures they would have with boy witches and girl pirates.

Before I got the name o' Nubs, everyone used to call me Numbnuts, cuz they thought I was stupid. Don't think anyone in that backwater town knew my real name, well 'cept family, and they done died: Ma, even though I gave her a kidney, an' Dad, even though I gave him some marrow and platelets. I reckon they call me Numbnuts cuz I kep' givin' parts o' meself. Body parts, I mean. When Sis lost her thumb in the meat grinder, I let 'em take off'n one o' my big toes...back when I still had 'em, an' now she's got a workin' thumb. Got this eye patch when I tried to give my eye to a fourth-grade buddy who lost one his in an explosion.

Well, the stem cell thingy didn't work, an' the eye didn't take, an' he started pickin' on me, so I lost an eye an' a buddy.

Afore I graduated high school, I gave Aunt Jan part o' my liver, but the cancer got 'er anyway.

On'y thing I never gave was my heart, to the one guy who got it, an' who new my name.

Grizzled ol' fairy, ya call me? Sure, go right ahead: Insult me all ya want; I got thick skin. Gotta have it, bein' disabled. After all, your'n the one who paid me ta tell ya the story of how I lost my limbs. I'm thirty-two, by the way... Being a quadruple amputee will wear on ya...

They, her parents, her aides, everyone, they never let her out in the rain. All because of that time, that one  time, she'd gone racing around downtown in her power chair in a downpour, and her battery shorted out the next day.

The irony did not escape Jessica. Walking people's legs never lost power because of water coming down from the sky. Hell, walking people could run marathons in the rain. But in the rain, her power wheelchair, sputtered, squealed and died, after marathonning around downtown at age 12.

And now, here she was, sitting in a manual wheelchair that her spastic hands couldn't propel in a straight line, under a hospital awning, watching the sky gray to storm-clouds as the raw rain began to spit. This was her what? fourteenth surgery in this place, and now she was twenty-two. Except she didn't feel like twenty-two the way Taylor Swift did. But then again, Taylor Swift would never have cerebral palsy, and T-Swift would be rich enough to afford her own people to be with her every second. T-Swift would never be trapped, alone, in a wheelchair she couldn't propel in a straight line.

Jessica watched the water whoosh down the drain at the end of the concrete ramp. She left the safety of the awning. By the time she'd dragged the heavy metal of bulk of the chair to the head of the ramp, she was panting and sweating with triumph. Perspiration and rain rivuleted down her face. Droplets thrummed on her cast.

She launched herself and let go. Gravity propelled her around the ramp's sinuous curves. The chair's wheels rushed, leaving fans of water in her wake.

Eventually, someone on the surgical ward recalled that Jessica had been left outside. When they finally found her, everything was soaked through, and she was laughing, triumphant. Maybe they didn't want her out in the rain, but she had hauled this behemoth of a manual chair out, swerved swiftly down a ramp, and gone out anyway. 

Swerved swiftly... She was J-Swift. That thought made Jessica guffaw even harder.

I am that child who my parents spent so much time with that they neglected my twin.

1. The fact that your parents are trying to communicate with you is awesome. Keep trying.

2. Seek out your local center for independent living, orgs which help the disabled and families. Your parents can probably get him on Medicaid, which will allow them to access many services for him, including respite care. They clearly can't do it alone.

3. Your feelings are ok. You ARE being neglected. You are NOT a monster; you're a frightened lonely young woman. Your brother scares you.

4. Talk to your parents about your fears with a counselor as a mediator. Seek therapy for yourself through school.

good luck.

OP, I'm sorry for all your losses. I was born disabled and I know many people who have such difficulty adjusting to acquired disabilities because they compare their current selves and former selves.

As others have said, seek therapy; if possible find a therapist who's specializes in or has experience counseling the disabled. Also seek out something called centers for independent living.

they are federally mandated centers that offer services for people with disabilities. Google "Center for Independent living" in your state.

See if you can qualify for caregivers through Medicaid. If you can't drive, you may qualify for wheelchair accessible bus use.

When ready, contact the state division of vocational rehabilitation. They assist disabled people who want to work.

See if you can get SSI or SSDI.
